Man, the writing is wretched in some scenes. It’s laughably bad. It gets much better in the second half but the first half was Razzie worthy. Cruise and Kidman both take opportunities to do some of the worst acting in their careers. The party scene and high scene are almost unbearable acting. I’ve read some of the treatise and dissertation defenses about how this is the point but c’mon…”it’s a dream!”, “it’s Brechtian alienation effect”, “it’s a commentary on society.” Or, it’s just poorly acted at times under the direction of a drill sergeant who is micromanaging these very particular Hollywood stars who don’t know how to work with him. I love Kidman and I’m in no way a Cruise hater but yeesh. Cruise definitely gets better in the latter half when he has something to do besides walk around half mast looking for people to take to bone town. And Kidman pretty much disappears from the film. The colors are beautiful. Love what Kubrick and team did with the palette. Some cool locations and camerawork too. Was Kubrick killed by the cabal for this film? Honestly, I don’t think they really cared because this film’s reception for the layman was, “Kidman is naked a bunch. Let’s goooo!” rather than some Epstein-like conspiracy reveal. But it is a fun conspiracy theory to engage with. Someday, someone will sit me down and explain why this is a masterpiece. Until then, in my opinion, it is a gigantic whiff. We rarely suffer any physical harm from “betrayal.” Betrayal is something that is born in the heart, something that wounds the heart. And it’s incredibly difficult to grasp what betrayal actually is. Perhaps betrayal only comes into existence when either you or the other person feels that something is “betrayal.” That’s how I think it works. Betrayal can exist even without any action behind it, and in essence, it is just as much a betrayal as one that involves an actual act. If both are guilty, then perhaps neither is. Surely, everyone lives with countless betrayals inside themselves that they never actually act upon. And perhaps that is why, when we ourselves are betrayed, we suffer from the fact that we have no choice but to forgive the other person as someone who is guilty of the very same thing we are. And because it hurts, we close our eyes to it. Both of us. The movie does feel somewhat drawn-out overall, but I found it interesting how it makes you feel that everything that happens between people ultimately happens inside their hearts. Perhaps I felt that even more strongly because the two leads, who are both beautiful yet somehow strangely devoid of sex appeal, seemed almost like empty “vessels.”

RATING: Below Average (4/10) My initial takeaway is that I’m heavily concerned this is one of my brother’s favorite movies. For context, whether it makes me prude or conservative, I’m not a massive fan of extensive nudity in films. I prefer to keep my box office and boobs separate. I also couldn’t appreciate the messaging from Kubrick due to the constant sexual undertones and overall “cuck energy”. The film also lacks a cohesive plot and rather aimlessly follows Cruise’s character, really only displaying his prowess and range as an actor. His performance makes me wish a top tier director would cast him for a film outside his current action blockbusters. Sydney Pollack felt flat and lackluster while Nicole Kidman was exploited and one dimensional in an unremarkable supporting cast. On a high note, the cult mansion scene was executed perfectly, finding myself heavily invested in the intoxicating atmosphere. This act highlighted the simple, jarring score, setting a precedent for building suspense. I did feel satisfied with the ending as in a convoluted way, it tied the lack of plot together. While I’d never watch it again, I could see the appeal to a certain audience as it emulates a Walmart-version Midsommar.

The fact that is film has not garnered more attention in a post Epstein era is more terrifying than the film itself. The score was so simple yet so haunting and the piano was so unsettling even just by alternating between two notes. Normally I would say some light-hearted things about the movie I just watched. And I’ll say same at the end, but for now I am going to keep things serious. Because this was a serious movie. The wheels in my head are still turning about the meaning behind what I’ve watched, below the surface of what we are told. It’s a dangerous movie, that is for sure. I can only imagine what was within the 40 cut minutes of this film, which were destroyed after Kubrick’s death. It almost feels like a warning to how the uppermost people of the world exist. It’s scary because it could be true. Key word “could”. Some films are scary because we know they are real somewhere, but this one is purely unknown. Alas, how unknown is it really, how far-fetched do the events in this film actually seem? This is what Kubrick seemed to want to show us with his final film. To tell us to keep our Eyes Wide Open in a corrupt world that thrives on us keeping them Shut. However, this what I feel could be an underlying theme. Obviously this film is based on an older novella as I discovered, which shares a different message. Just as interesting though. Tom Cruise did wonders in this film, can’t wait to see him in Digger. The ambiance was unbelievably tense, that piano was dreadful, in a good way. The dialogue and scenes were so encapsulating. Truly a work of art. Finally as promised, a lighter paragraph. If Die Hard and Gremlins are Christmas movies (for the record I think they both are), is Eyes Wide Shut as well? Food for thought.

Still such an amazing film, with incredible performances from Kidman and Cruise! I hate when people say sex shouldn’t be in films, because this movie makes a pretty strong argument for why it can be an important part of storytelling. It isn’t there just for the sake of being provocative; it actually plays an important role in the story, the characters, and the themes the film is exploring.I especially love watching Bill change throughout the film. Every time I rewatch it, I notice more about his journey and how the events of the night slowly challenge the way he sees himself, his marriage, and the world around him. Cruise does such a fantastic job showing that change. Kubrick’s direction is incredible, and there’s something so hypnotic about the way this entire movie is filmed. The atmosphere, the cinematography, the music, and the pacing all come together to create an experience that feels completely unique. Kidman and Cruise are both fantastic, and watching them share the screen makes the film even more fascinating. Their performances feel incredibly committed, and there’s so much going on beneath the surface of their characters. I also can’t help but think about how much of a financial risk a film like this would be today. A major studio probably wouldn’t take the same kind of chances on a movie this strange, slow, ambitious, and adult-oriented.
